t081.sum: Marriage is human society's institutional response to the biologic fact of bisexuality, and the home is the crowning fruit of that long evolutionary struggle. The Urantia Book says that marriage is not a sacrament but an essentially human institution, yet it teaches that pair marriage and the good home are the roots of civilization's stability and of morality, and the place where the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man are first learned.
t081.s1.h: The Origin and Social Meaning of Marriage
t081.s1.i1: Marriage is not the mating instinct itself but the institutional reaction society developed to regulate that instinct.
t081.s1.i3: Marriage always has an outer domain regulated by mores and law and a private, personal domain between man and woman.
t081.s1.i4: Marriage has always been bound up with property and religion: property stabilized marriage, and religion moralized it.
t081.s1.i5: Material necessity founded marriage, sex appetite embellished it, religion sanctioned it, and love later came to justify it.
t081.s1.i6: Intelligently adjusting the strong sex urge to social regulation is the supreme test of the reality of civilization, and it always demands self-control.
t081.s2.i1: Monogamy is not natural to evolving man at first, but it has great cultural value and is unquestionably best for the children.
t081.s2.i3: The ideal of pair marriage entails self-denial, so it often fails when the partners lack rugged self-control.
t081.s2.i4: Monogamy fosters delicate sentiments, refinement of moral character, and spiritual growth, and is best for the happiness of parents and the welfare of children.
t081.s2.i5: Society should not ignore the plight of those who fail to obtain mates but should always treat them with kindness and consideration.
t081.s3.h: A Human Institution, Not a Sacrament
t081.s3.i2: Comparing the union of husband and wife to the relation of the Adjuster and man, or to a divine union, is an unfortunate analogy that has caused great confusion.
t081.s3.i3: The very fact that marriage can be dissolved shows that God is not a party to the union.
t081.s3.i4: Yet there is an ideal of marriage on the high spheres, embodied supremely by the Material Sons and Daughters; ideal mortal marriage is humanly sacred.
t081.s3.i5: The marriage ideals of youth should not be crushed, but they should be balanced by learning the realities of home life beforehand, with a degree of disillusionment.
t081.s4.i1: Religious, social, and educational institutions are needed, but since children learn most essentials of life from home and neighborhood, the home is the chief civilizing agency.
t081.s4.i4: Man and woman can never fully understand each other, but they complement each other effectively, and their differences continue into the morontia and spirit careers.
t081.s4.i5: Marriage is now passing beyond the stage that regarded the wife as property into a new era that respects personality.
t081.s5.h: Parents, Children, and the Spiritual Meaning of the Home
t081.s5.i1: Bearing children is not a parental right but the supreme responsibility of human existence; civilization places duties on parents and rights on children.
t081.s5.i2: The home is the basic unit of brotherhood, where parents and children together learn the patience, altruism, tolerance, and forbearance that brotherhood requires.
t081.s5.i3: Society would be greatly improved by returning to the practice of the family council, as among the Andites, where family affairs were discussed freely and fraternally.
t081.s5.i5: Jesus said the gospel of the kingdom would be better received when understood in family terms, as the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man.
t081.s5.i6: Jesus taught that the true family rests on seven facts: existence, safety and pleasure, education, discipline, companionship, love and mercy, and provision for the future.
t081.s5.i7: After Joseph's death the young Jesus made the support of the family his first duty and acted as a father to his brothers and sisters.
t081.s6.i1: The greatest threat to family life is the modern pleasure mania that pursues self-gratification.
t081.s6.i3: Wholesome play and recreation have value, but pleasure that brings the breakup of marriage and the home is self-destructive.
t081.s6.i4: Attempts to shift parental responsibility to the state or the church would be suicidal to the welfare and progress of civilization.
t082.sum: Civilization is a racial acquirement that mankind won through a long and arduous struggle, starting from a state close to the animal. Because it is not passed on automatically by heredity, each generation must hand it on anew through the home and education. The Urantia Book examines one by one the material, intellectual, and social factors that sustain civilization, yet it says that the power that truly lifts culture is spiritual idealism.
t082.s1.i2: Scientific, philosophic, and religious achievements are not inherited; they are kept only by wisely conserving social inheritance and educating each generation anew.
t082.s1.i3: Biologic evolution and cultural civilization do not necessarily go together, but culture cannot flourish without a background of adequate racial progress.
t082.s1.i4: Even though the missions of Caligastia and Adam failed, evolution kept the races moving forward; evolution may be delayed but it cannot be stopped.
t082.s1.i5: The slogan "back to nature" is an ignorant delusion based on belief in a golden age that never existed.
t082.s2.i1: Primitive man was not naturally brotherly; through bitter experience he learned that to survive he must unite, and so he cooperated reluctantly.
t082.s2.i2: Civilization became man's insurance against violent death, and man pays the premium by submitting to society's mores.
t082.s2.i3: Hunger, sex love, vanity, and fear of ghosts drew people together and bound them into society.
t082.s2.i5: The one hundred of Dalamatia did not try to change the primitive races all at once but trained the best of the tribes and sent them back as emissaries of social uplift.
t082.s2.i6: The chief purpose of the Material Sons and Daughters is to move evolving man from the hunting and herding stages to the agricultural stage.
t082.s3.i1: Factors such as the natural environment, capital goods, scientific knowledge, human resources, language, machines, and the coordination of experts sustain present civilization.
t082.s3.i3: Science stabilizes philosophy by eliminating error and purifies religion by destroying superstition.
t082.s3.i4: A common language promotes peace and insures culture, and international exchange in language, trade, art, science, and religion should be encouraged.
t082.s3.i5: Science guided by wisdom can liberate mankind, but it becomes a calamity for nations lacking the wisdom to adjust the transitional problems of mechanization.
t082.s4.i1: The basic institution for passing the torch of culture to the next generation is the home, followed by play, social life, and the school.
t082.s4.i3: Intelligence controls the machinery of civilization and wisdom directs it, but the energy that lifts culture from level to level is spiritual idealism.
t082.s4.i5: High civilization is born when material wealth, intellectual greatness, moral worth, social cleverness, and cosmic insight are wisely coordinated.
t082.s4.i6: Civilization is jeopardized only when able and wise leadership disappears, and such leadership has never exceeded one per cent of the population.
t082.s5.i1: Cultural society is not a club of free memberships but a union of workers making a better world for their descendants.
t082.s5.i2: Every right is linked with social obligation, and liberty that accepts collective regulation is the legitimate goal of social evolution.
t082.s5.i4: Society is not a divine institution but a phenomenon of evolution, so it may be experimented with fearlessly, but great changes should not be attempted suddenly.
t082.s5.i5: Modern civilization has grown intellectually and scientifically but has stagnated in ethical awareness, spiritual development, and the safeguarding of the home.
t082.s6.i1: Religion renders its highest social service when least entangled with secular institutions, and it should not directly engage in building a new order or preserving the old.
t082.s6.i2: As civilization advances, the attitude of seeking first heavenly realities becomes all the more necessary, even amid efforts to solve material problems.
t082.s6.i3: Modern culture must become spiritually baptized with a new revelation of Jesus' life.
t083.sum: Government was not designed by anyone; it is an institution that evolved through trial and error in efforts to adjust human antagonisms and keep the peace. The Urantia Book traces its development from the council of elders to modern representative government and names the separation of executive, legislative, and judicial functions as the only sacred feature of government. It teaches that a state can never rise above the moral values of its citizens, and that true world peace will come when a government of all mankind is established.
t083.s1.i1: Once man had partly solved the problem of making a living, he faced the task of regulating human relations, and private property made government necessary.
t083.s1.i4: Peace groups widened from the family to the clan, the tribe, and the nation, and then to the territorial state, now embracing many nations beyond ties of blood.
t083.s1.i5: The first organ of government was the council of elders, which already contained the seeds of executive, legislative, and judicial functions.
t083.s2.h: Rights, Justice, and the Gifts of Society
t083.s2.i1: Nature confers no rights on man, and the supreme gift of society to man is security.
t083.s2.i2: Natural justice is a man-made theory; the only justice nature gives is the unfailing conformity of results to causes.
t083.s2.i3: Liberty is a gift of civilization made possible by the enforcement of law; for one person to be absolutely free, another must be a slave.
t083.s2.i4: The chief task of government is to define what is right, regulate class differences fairly, and enforce equality of opportunity under the rule of law.
t083.s3.h: Representative Government and the Separation of Powers
t083.s3.i1: Universe administrators have learned by experience that evolutionary peoples are best governed by representative government with three balanced branches.
t083.s3.i3: Mortals must create their own government and constitution and choose the ablest and most worthy as their leaders and judges.
t083.s3.i5: Democracy carries dangers such as the glorification of mediocrity, the choice of ignorant rulers, and enslavement to public opinion.
t083.s3.i6: Educating public opinion is the only safe way to accelerate civilization, and voting is the right method even when doing the wrong thing.
t083.s4.i1: What the state does matters more than its form of government, and no state can rise above the moral values of its citizens.
t083.s4.i2: The ideal state is moved by three impulses: the love loyalty born of realizing brotherhood, wise patriotism, and cosmic insight.
t083.s4.i4: In advanced states political service is honored as the highest devotion of the citizen, and public office is regarded as an honor, not a burden.
t083.s4.i5: An enduring state is founded on culture, ruled by ideals, and motivated by service, and its education aims at wisdom and spiritual values.
t083.s4.i6: An economy of profit motivation alone is doomed unless supplemented by service motives, yet it must not be abolished suddenly before higher motives are established.
t083.s4.i7: A continental nation on a neighboring planet, with a federation of one hundred states and a three-branch representative government, has a society more advanced than Urantia's.
t083.s5.i1: Relative sovereignty exists on only two levels, the spiritual free will of the individual and the collective sovereignty of mankind as a whole; all groups between are temporary.
t083.s5.i3: Even if all weapons were abolished, nations clinging to the illusion of national sovereignty would fight with fists and stones.
t083.s5.i4: The Most Highs rule in the kingdoms of men to bring about the greatest good for all men, not for any chosen people.
t083.s6.i1: Sonship in the kingdom should make believers better citizens of earthly nations, and believers bear a twofold duty to God and to man.
t083.s6.i2: Believers must not worship temporal rulers nor try to extend the spiritual kingdom by temporal power.
t083.s6.i3: The persistent spread of the gospel will in time separate politics from religion and bring intellectual and religious liberty to all peoples.
t084.sum: The bestowal of Jesus is the event in which Michael, Creator Son of Nebadon, in his seventh and final bestowal, was born on Urantia as a mortal infant and lived a human life to its end. Through this bestowal Michael completed his universe sovereignty by experience and ended the Lucifer rebellion; above all, he revealed God to man and showed God a man made perfect. The Urantia Book stresses that the supreme purpose of the bestowal was to enhance the revelation of God.
t084.s1.h: Seven Bestowals and Sovereignty Earned by Experience
t084.s1.i1: A Creator Son must live the life of his creatures in their likeness, and this is part of the price paid for universe sovereignty.
t084.s1.i2: After six bestowals, as a Melchizedek, a Lanonandek, an Adam, a seraphim, a mortal, and a morontia mortal, Michael became a mortal of flesh and blood on Urantia in his seventh.
t084.s1.i4: In each bestowal Michael subjected himself to a different will of the Paradise Deities, and on Urantia he submitted wholly to the will of the Universal Father.
t084.s1.i5: The sum of the seven bestowals became Nebadon's new revelation of the Supreme Being and also contributed to expanding the sovereignty of the Supreme.
t084.s1.i6: The Eternal Son shares creature experience through the incarnations of the Paradise Sons, and so in Michael he actually came to mortal man.
t084.s2.i1: Unlike his earlier bestowals, Michael had to appear on Urantia not as a fully grown being but as a helpless infant.
t084.s2.i2: Michael was to lay aside all extraplanetary help and live his mortal life relying only on the Paradise Father.
t084.s2.i4: Immanuel advised him to be chiefly a teacher, first liberating man's spiritual nature, enlightening his mind, and freeing him from age-old fears.
t084.s2.i5: He was also counseled not to become involved in economic and political matters, not to form an organized cult, and to leave no writings or portraits.
t084.s2.i6: Since a bestowal Son leaves no human offspring on a planet, Jesus would not enter the marriage relation.
t084.s3.i1: One goal of the bestowal was, as the Son of Man, to formally terminate the Lucifer rebellion in Satania and be recognized as the Planetary Prince of Urantia.
t084.s3.i2: His life was intended less as an example for the people of Urantia than as an inspiration for all generations in all of Nebadon.
t084.s3.i3: He revealed the Father to the creatures of flesh and at the same time showed God a new revelation of man.
t084.s3.i4: He was charged to pour out the Spirit of Truth at the end of his bestowal, so that all normal mortals would have immediate access to the ministry of the Adjusters.
t084.s3.i6: His life of self-forgetful service forever silenced those who had charged the Creators with selfishly holding on to power.
t084.s4.i2: Jesus did not gradually become God, nor did he become man at some moment; he was always God and man, and what grew was his awareness of that fact.
t084.s4.i3: A bestowal in which a Paradise Son appears in the world by natural processes is the most fascinating of miracles even to local universe citizens.
t084.s5.i1: Jesus passed through every stage of human life from infancy to death and personally experienced a wide range of emotions, from joy to deep sorrow.
t084.s5.i2: He did not set a detailed example for all to copy but lived a truly human life so that each person could live his own life in his own time.
t084.s5.i3: His life fully revealed God to man and offered God a perfected human personality, and it was wholly accepted by the Father.
t084.s5.i5: At his baptism in the Jordan he was a perfected mortal at the height of mind mastery, and his Adjuster stood by him as a Personalized Adjuster instead of fusing.
t084.s6.i1: Having completed the Urantia bestowal, Michael was recognized by the Ancients of Days and the Universal Father as the settled ruler of Nebadon.
t084.s6.i2: Your little world has become known throughout Nebadon as the place where the Creator Son completed the experience required for sovereignty.
t085.sum: In The Urantia Book's portrayal of the character of Jesus, the most distinctive feature is not so much flawlessness as symmetry, the exquisite and balanced unification of all his qualities. He was enthusiastic but never fanatical, courageous but never foolhardy, full of gladness yet humble. At the center stood a childlike trust in God and a deep love for people, and he asked his followers not so much to believe in him as to believe with him.
t085.s1.i2: An ordinary mortal cannot attain Jesus' perfection of character, but it is altogether possible to develop a strong and unified personality along the lines of his.
t085.s1.i3: He was emotional but not flighty, sympathetic but not sentimental, pious but not sanctimonious.
t085.s1.i4: His plans were marked by consecrated common sense, with nothing queer, erratic, or hysterical about them.
t085.s1.i5: As a perfectly unified personality, Jesus still today unifies human experience and simplifies life.
t085.s2.i1: He was free from affectation and hypocrisy and lived as he taught, staying true to the truth even when his sincerity brought him suffering.
t085.s2.i2: He was frank but always kind; he hated sin but loved the sinner, and in all his honesty he was fair.
t085.s2.i4: Even when urged, he did not hurry, saying his hour had not yet come; when indignant at evil, his anger was never directed at the sinner.
t085.s2.i5: He did not seek popular support and was not swayed by people's opinions; he was brave but never proud.
t085.s3.i2: He was not a blind optimist, but out of trust in God and confidence in man he always encouraged others to be of good cheer.
t085.s3.i3: Jesus was a child of joy and a man of rare humor, and at the same time a man acquainted with sorrow.
t085.s3.i4: Graciousness is the aroma of friendliness from a love-saturated soul, and Jesus spread that gladness wherever he went.
t085.s3.i5: He was always generous, repeating that it is more blessed to give than to receive, but he was never wasteful or extravagant.
t085.s4.i1: Because Jesus truly understood people, he showed genuine sympathy, yet he never indulged in pity or fostered their self-pity.
t085.s4.i2: He never hurried and comforted people "as he passed by"; they felt they were consulting with him rather than confessing to him.
t085.s4.i3: He did not try to direct or manage people, and those who received his smile felt their power to solve their own problems increase.
t085.s4.i4: Great things happened because people not only believed in him but he also believed greatly in them.
t085.s4.i6: The apostles remembered him as a loyal friend who treated all with equal kindness without flattery, and who loved even sinners and enemies.
t085.s5.i1: Jesus' faith was not tradition or intellectual belief but wholly personal and spiritual, born of experience with the indwelling Adjuster.
t085.s5.i2: He did not hold faith as a consolation in hardship but enjoyed it as the serenity and thrill of living in the Father's presence.
t085.s5.i4: His strong faith never turned into fanaticism and was always in harmony with balanced judgment about family love, social obligation, and economic necessity.
t085.s5.i5: His sublime self-forgetfulness shows in his reply when called good teacher: "Why do you call me good?"
t085.s6.h: What It Means to Follow Him
t085.s6.i1: Jesus did not ask his disciples to believe in him but to believe with him in the love of God.
t085.s6.i2: To follow Jesus means to share his faith and to take part in his spirit of unselfish service to men.
t085.s6.i3: A great service of this revelation will be to bring back the living Jesus, the human Jesus buried in theological tradition.
t086.sum: The teachings of Jesus are rooted in the simple gospel that God is the Father of all men and that men, recognizing by faith that they are his sons, become brothers to one another. The kingdom of heaven is not a political realm but a spiritual experience that begins within each person, and faith opens its door. Jesus gave the new commandment to love not merely as one loves oneself but as he loved, and he called people out of the religion of tradition and authority into the religion of the spirit that knows God directly.
t086.s1.i2: Jesus taught a new concept of God, not as a judge keeping a ledger of sins but as a Father who loves each person.
t086.s1.i3: The kingdom of heaven is built on the truths of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, and this teaching frees man from age-old animal fears.
t086.s1.i4: Jesus said that people of other ages would better understand the gospel if it were presented in terms of family relationships rather than of a kingdom.
t086.s1.i5: His gospel delivered man from the superstition that he is a child of the devil and lifted him to the dignity of a faith son of God.
t086.s2.i1: Jesus said the kingdom of heaven had nothing to do with earthly kingdoms or temporal governments, but the idea of a temporal king rooted deep in the Jewish mind was not easily removed.
t086.s2.i3: Simple, childlike faith is the key that opens the door of the kingdom; once inside, one must grow through the steps of righteousness.
t086.s2.i4: God's forgiveness is actually experienced in the measure that a person forgives his fellows.
t086.s2.i5: The kingdom is an evolutionary experience that begins on earth and advances through successive stages of life to Paradise.
t086.s3.i1: Brotherly love is loving one's neighbor as oneself, but fatherly love is loving people as Jesus loved them.
t086.s3.i2: Disciples should strive to see people as God sees them and so begin to show fatherly affection.
t086.s3.i4: The new commandment is not a new burden but meant to bring the new joy of sharing affection with one's fellows.
t086.s3.i5: "Resist not evil" did not mean condoning sin but forgiving rather than retaliating against personal insults.
t086.s4.i1: Jesus said not to patch new teaching onto the old but to be born again like little children and make a fresh start.
t086.s4.i2: The righteousness he required is not buying favor through alms, prayer, and fasting, but the desire to do the Father's will in love, mercy, and truth.
t086.s4.i3: The greatest discovery a human soul can make is to find God within and to make that a fact of personal experience.
t086.s4.i5: Jesus did not teach that all should think alike; believers are united in their diversity by the motive and goal of doing the Father's will.
t086.s5.i1: Always respect human personality, and never sweep people into the kingdom by overpowering them with logic, eloquence, fear, or sentiment.
t086.s5.i2: The gospel restores self-respect to those who have lost it and restrains those who have too much.
t086.s5.i3: The teaching to trust God is not passive fatalism; what Jesus opposed was not forethought but worry and anxiety.
t086.s5.i4: His teaching was not the talk of a meek mystic but dynamic; he not only meant well but actually did good.
t086.s6.i2: The gospel of the kingdom rests on Jesus' own religious experience, while Christianity rests mainly on Paul's.
t086.s6.i3: As the Messiah of the kingdom became the Redeemer of the church, Jesus' teachings were transplanted from Jewish to gentile soil.
t086.s6.i4: The Spirit of Truth restates Jesus' message anew for each generation, helping it remember and understand his teachings.
t087.sum: The parable is the storytelling method of teaching that Jesus first used with the multitude by the Sea of Galilee and that thereafter became almost his only method of public instruction. He taught that parables should not be interpreted as allegories with a hidden meaning in every detail but received as true-to-life stories that reveal one central truth. A parable appeals at once to minds of different levels, plants new truth while avoiding prejudice and controversy, and leaves each person to find its meaning in his own soul.
t087.s1.h: The Beginning of Teaching by Parables
t087.s1.i1: Jesus first used this method when, from a boat by the sea, he told the parable of the sower to a crowd of nearly a thousand.
t087.s1.i2: It was intended that those sincerely wishing to enter the kingdom would grasp the meaning, while those seeking to entrap him would see and not understand.
t087.s1.i3: From then on Jesus taught the public almost entirely in parables and explained their meaning more fully to the apostles in the evening.
t087.s1.i4: Parables appealing to nature were the best reply to the charge that his work was done by the power of the devil, and they gave his enemies less to seize upon.
t087.s2.i1: Peter and Nathaniel disagreed while interpreting the parable of the sower as an allegory with a hidden meaning in every detail.
t087.s2.i2: Thomas recalled the Master's teaching that illustrations should use true-to-life stories that reveal one central truth.
t087.s2.i4: Jesus said that private flights of imagination may be profitable, but offering them as public teaching is a mistake.
t087.s2.i5: Jesus advised avoiding fables and allegories and using parables freely, especially those drawn from nature.
t087.s3.i3: The parable plants new truth in the mind while bypassing prejudice and arousing a minimum of antagonism.
t087.s3.i4: Parables avoid direct conflict with tradition and authority and recall the teaching whenever the familiar scene is seen again.
t087.s3.i5: Hearing the same story, each person can interpret a parable according to his own intellectual and spiritual level.
t087.s4.i1: The parable of the sower reviewed the ministry up to then and foreshadowed the varied success later messengers would meet.
t087.s4.i2: Appealing only to emotion or intellect bears no fruit; true change of character comes from appealing to the spirit that lives within man.
t087.s4.i3: The parable of the seed that grows by itself into the full ear shows that the kingdom grows quietly beyond human understanding.
t087.s4.i4: The parables of the mustard seed and the leaven tell how the kingdom, small in its beginnings, grows great and spreads like leaven through the whole lump.
t087.s5.i3: The father of the prodigal saw his son returning afar off, ran to meet him, and ordered a feast before the son had finished his confession.
t087.s5.i4: The three stories of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son show respectively the Father seeking the lost, the thoroughness of the search, and complete restoration.
t087.s5.i5: The parable of the prodigal son and the story of the good Samaritan were Jesus' favorite ways of teaching the Father's love and human neighborliness.
t087.s6.i1: To the trick question "Who is my neighbor?" Jesus answered with the story of the good Samaritan, letting the lawyer answer for himself.
t087.s6.i2: The parable of the Pharisee and the publican teaches that salvation cannot be bought by works but is a free gift to all who have faith.
t087.s6.i3: The parables of the talents and the pounds show that ability is the measure of opportunity and that equal faithfulness receives equal reward.
t088.sum: In the wilderness Jesus decided not to win people's attention and allegiance by miracles and wonders, and he kept that decision to the end. Yet because one with unlimited creator prerogatives was on earth, filled with divine mercy and human sympathy, extraordinary events such as healings sometimes followed apart from his will. The Urantia Book shows that many events that seemed miraculous were in fact natural occurrences, and it explains that even genuine miracles did not break natural law but involved the elimination of the time factor.
t088.s1.h: The Decision Not to Work Miracles
t088.s1.i1: During the forty days in the wilderness Jesus resolved not to use universe power to satisfy the Jewish craving for signs.
t088.s1.i3: Wonder-working only stirs the material mind to outward allegiance; it neither reveals God nor saves men.
t088.s1.i5: He did not break this decision even when the Pharisees demanded proof or when he was taunted at Calvary to come down from the cross.
t088.s2.i1: At the wedding feast at Cana others expected a miracle, but the most surprised of all was Jesus himself, who had resolved not to work one.
t088.s2.i3: The agents of the Creator made wine by the ordinary natural processes, only independently of time.
t088.s2.i4: It would not have happened had it been contrary to the Father's will, since Jesus had already committed all things to the Father's will.
t088.s3.i1: The great catch of fish was no miracle; Jesus, a skilled fisherman who knew the habits of fish, simply told them where the school was.
t088.s3.i2: The healing of Peter's mother-in-law's fever was not a miracle either, but a miracle-seeking generation counted all such coincidences as miracles.
t088.s3.i3: Jesus encouraged the apostles not to attribute ordinary physical events to spiritual causes but to seek the true causes of all phenomena.
t088.s3.i4: The rabbis regarded blindness from birth as the result of sin, but Jesus rejected such superstitious explanations.
t088.s4.h: The Sundown Healing and Genuine Miracles
t088.s4.i1: At Capernaum, when Jesus said he wished his children to be made whole if it was not contrary to the Father's will, 683 persons were healed in a moment.
t088.s4.i2: Jesus himself was the most surprised by this healing, having momentarily forgotten the warning that he could not limit the time element of creator prerogatives.
t088.s4.i4: The cleansing of the leper was the first so-called miracle Jesus performed intentionally.
t088.s4.i6: When Jesus thanked the Father at the raising of Lazarus, the celestial hosts acted, and Lazarus came to life in twelve seconds of earth time.
t088.s5.i1: Of the five thousand fed by the miracle, only about five hundred continued to follow Jesus.
t088.s5.i2: Jesus said he would not turn from his mission of revealing the Father to satisfy the curiosity of wonder-seekers.
t088.s5.i3: The fame of his healings brought prejudice-raising publicity and unsought notoriety, causing Jesus much trouble.
t088.s5.i4: The resurrection of Lazarus strengthened the faith of believers, but the religious leaders hastened their decision to destroy Jesus.
t088.s6.i1: To local universe citizens there are few miracles, and the most intriguing of them are the incarnational bestowals of the Paradise Sons.
t088.s6.i3: Even in all these extraordinary experiences the Father chose to reveal himself in normal, natural, and dependable ways.
t089.sum: The twelve apostles were ordinary Galileans whom Jesus personally called, trained, and ordained to proclaim the gospel of the kingdom of heaven. They were not ignorant men but men of varied temperaments who had received synagogue schooling, and each, with his own strengths and weaknesses, was transformed by living with Jesus. That only one of them deserted him, even though Jesus repeatedly shattered their worldly expectations, testifies to the charm of his life.
t089.s1.i1: Jesus chose the first six himself, and each of them recommended one more, making twelve.
t089.s1.i2: The first six apostles went out two by two, preaching the gospel by personal contact, and learned that religion is a purely personal experience.
t089.s1.i3: The monotonous period of alternating fishing and personal work was a severe test, but they endured it through loyalty to the Master.
t089.s1.i4: On January 12, A.D. 27, Jesus ordained the twelve as public preachers of the gospel of the kingdom.
t089.s1.i5: The so-called Sermon on the Mount was not the gospel itself but Jesus' ordination charge to the twelve.
t089.s2.i2: "Unlearned" means they were laymen untrained in rabbinical lore and methods of scriptural interpretation.
t089.s2.i3: The apostles learned about the kingdom of heaven from Jesus, and Jesus learned much about human nature from them.
t089.s2.i4: All the apostles loved Jesus, but each was drawn by some trait of his character that especially appealed to him.
t089.s3.i1: Andrew, the eldest, became chief of the apostolic corps and held that place to the end; not a great preacher, he was an effective personal worker.
t089.s3.i2: Peter was impulsive and optimistic, a born leader and eloquent speaker, but his speech often ran ahead of his thinking.
t089.s3.i3: James Zebedee had a fierce temper, but his ability to see a problem from many sides brought him closest to the real meaning of Jesus' teaching.
t089.s3.i4: John, the youngest, served as Jesus' personal representative in many matters, but the phrase "the disciple whom Jesus loved" is not accurate.
t089.s3.i5: Peter, James, and John were appointed by Andrew as personal aides to attend to Jesus at his side.
t089.s4.i1: Philip, with his "show me," lacked imagination but was a faithful steward who did small things in a great way.
t089.s4.i2: Nathaniel was an honest man "in whom there is no guile" and the philosopher of the twelve; his weakness was a pride that verged on prejudice.
t089.s4.i3: Matthew, the former publican, handled the finances of the group and was most deeply grateful for the Master's forgiving nature.
t089.s4.i4: Thomas was the real scientist of the group, with an analytic mind and unflinching courage, but he struggled with doubt all his life.
t089.s4.i5: The Alpheus twins were ordinary men with neither strong nor weak points, yet through them many timid believers entered the kingdom.
t089.s4.i6: Simon Zelotes led the hesitant into the kingdom by his inspiring loyalty, but he never fully shed his nationalistic thinking.
t089.s5.i1: Judas was the only Judean among the apostles and the best educated; he handled the treasury honestly and efficiently.
t089.s5.i3: He never overcame his prejudice against his Galilean associates and inwardly criticized Jesus as timid.
t089.s6.i1: Jesus told the apostles that, as citizens of another, heavenly kingdom, they must now live better lives than before.
t089.s6.i2: He taught the apostles at length not so much what they should do as what they should be.
t090.sum: Jesus died on the cross at Golgotha on a Friday in A.D. 30. The Urantia Book makes clear that this death was not an atoning sacrifice to appease the wrath of God or pay mankind's debt; it was not required by the Father but planned and carried out by man. The true meaning of the cross lies not in the fact of his death but in the manner and spirit in which he met it, the supreme expression of a love that forgave even enemies, and so the cross became the eternal symbol of unselfish service.
t090.s1.i1: When he was arrested, Jesus knew his work in the flesh was finished and took little interest in the details of the so-called trials.
t090.s1.i2: He did not answer false testimony, but he always answered the question whether he was the Son of God.
t090.s1.i3: Convinced that it was the Father's will for him to follow the natural course of events like an ordinary man, he did not try to change the outcome by his eloquence.
t090.s1.i4: He was crucified at about half past nine on Friday morning, and the unseen hosts of the universe watched in silence as the Creator underwent a creature's death.
t090.s2.i2: Though thirsty, Jesus refused the drugged wine offered to deaden his suffering.
t090.s2.i3: Unlike the brigand who mocked him, the other brigand turned wholeheartedly in his last hours and found salvation.
t090.s2.i4: As a sandstorm darkened the sky, Jesus cried, "It is finished," commended his spirit to the Father, and breathed his last.
t090.s2.i5: A Roman centurion who saw him die confessed that he truly was a Son of God.
t090.s3.i1: Jesus did not die to atone for the racial guilt of mankind or to provide a way of approach to an offended God.
t090.s3.i2: His death was neither a ransom to buy man back from fallen rulers nor a sacrifice to pay mankind's debt to God.
t090.s3.i3: The whole idea of ransom and atonement is incompatible with the concept of God as a loving Father, which Jesus taught and showed.
t090.s3.i4: Sin is not passed from parents to children; it is conscious rebellion committed by individual will creatures.
t090.s3.i5: Even a sovereign of justice would not be satisfied with the childish scheme of substituting an innocent person for the guilty.
t090.s4.i2: There is no direct connection between his death and the Jewish Passover sacrificial system.
t090.s4.i3: The experience required by the bestowal was already complete at his baptism; the manner of his later life and death was his personal ministry for his creatures.
t090.s4.i4: The gospel of realizing sonship with God by faith does not depend on his death and was illuminated even more by his life than by his death.
t090.s4.i5: The Father loved mankind just as much before Jesus lived and died as after.
t090.s5.h: The True Meaning of the Cross
t090.s5.i3: Divine love does not merely forgive wrongs; it absorbs and actually destroys them, so the forgiveness of love transcends the forgiveness of mercy.
t090.s5.i4: Jesus bore the cross of mortal existence for more than twenty-five years, and Golgotha was the final expression of that love.
t090.s5.i6: He lived and died not for this world alone but for the whole universe, and his death illuminated the certainty of survival after the death of the flesh.
t090.s6.i1: His love that laid down his life for his enemies was greater than any love then known on earth.
t090.s6.i2: The cross is not a symbol of substitution appeasing wrath but of unselfish service, in which the good bestow themselves on the evil to save them by love.
t090.s6.i3: Creatures on many worlds, looking upon Jesus on the cross, have not given up the struggle of faith but have pressed on once more.
t090.s6.i4: On the cross there was nothing the Father required, only what Jesus willingly gave and refused to avoid.
t090.s6.i5: His death was not meant to reconcile man to God but to awaken man to the Father's eternal love and the Son's mercy.
